title: Removal of Tractor Electrical and Electronic System Components and Parts

lessons.title: Safe removal of electrical parts
lessons.html:
Electrical parts on a tractor

Electrical parts include the battery, starter motor, alternator, lights, switches, relays, fuses, wiring harnesses and sensors. Modern tractors also have electronic control units (ECUs), displays and monitors. These parts are easy to damage if you remove them the wrong way.

First: disconnect the battery

  1. Make the tractor safe: level ground, handbrake on, key out.
  2. Wear safety glasses and gloves.
  3. Remove the negative battery lead first. Put it where it cannot touch the terminal.
  4. Then remove the positive lead if needed.

Some tractors have a battery isolator switch. Use it, but check with the mechanic if the battery leads must also come off. Some ECUs need the key to be off for a set time before disconnecting; follow the manual.

Removing the battery

Batteries are heavy and contain acid. Undo the clamp, lift with a battery carrier and keep it upright. Store it upright in the battery area. If acid spills, use the neutraliser and absorbent in the workshop spill kit.

Removing a starter or alternator

  • Take photos of the wires before removing them.
  • Label each wire with tape and a marker.
  • Undo the terminal nuts and put them back on their studs so they do not get lost.
  • For the alternator, loosen the belt tensioner first.
  • Support the starter; it is heavy and can fall when the last bolt comes out.

Lights and switches

Unplug the connector by pressing the lock tab. Never pull on the wires. Keep screws and clips in a labelled bag.

lessons.title: Connectors, harnesses and electronic units
lessons.html:
Handling connectors

Connectors have small pins and seals. Damage to them causes faults that are very hard to find later.

  • Find and press the locking tab or slide the lock before pulling.
  • Pull on the connector body, never on the wires.
  • Do not use screwdrivers to lever connectors apart.
  • Keep connectors clean and dry. Cover them with a plastic bag and tape if they will be open for long.
  • Look for green corrosion, bent pins or broken seals and tell the mechanic.

Removing a wiring harness

  1. Photograph the route of the harness.
  2. Label each connector at both ends with a tag.
  3. Cut cable ties carefully so you do not cut the wires.
  4. Note where the harness is clipped and where it passes through holes or grommets.
  5. Pull the harness out slowly. Do not drag it over sharp edges.
  6. Coil it loosely and store it in a clean box.

Sensors

Sensors measure things like temperature, pressure, speed and position. Unplug them before removing. Some sensors have O-rings; drain fluid first if needed. Speed and position sensors may have a set gap or position, so mark them before removing.

Electronic control units and displays

ECUs and displays are expensive. Handle them with care:

  • Remove them only when the mechanic says so.
  • Touch a bare metal part of the tractor first to release static electricity.
  • Do not touch the pins.
  • Store them in a dry, safe place, in a bag or box.
  • Label which tractor they came from. Many ECUs are programmed for one tractor.

Welding warning

If anyone will weld on the tractor, the battery and sometimes the ECUs must be disconnected first. Welding current can destroy electronic parts.

Record and report

Write on the job card all parts removed. Report damaged wires, chewed wires from rats, corrosion or burnt connectors.

Key points

  • Disconnect the battery negative lead first.
  • Photograph and label every wire and connector.
  • Press the lock tab and pull on the connector body, never the wires.
  • Handle ECUs carefully and label which tractor they came from.
  • Report corrosion, chewed or burnt wiring.
